Their not including it among their examples of OO is correct, since KRL wasn’t a part of Lisp but an extension on top of it—and was published later.
Still, a good paper, with some of CLU’s great contributions to the topic of modularity.
Timothy Jones, Michael Homer, James Noble, and Kim B. Bruce. Object Inheritance Without Classes. In Shriram Krishnamurthi and Benjamin S. Lerner (Ed.), Proc. 30th European Conference on Object-Oriented Programming (ECOOP 2016), Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs), 56. Schloss Dagstuhl – Leibniz-Zentrum für Informatik, Dagstuhl, Germany, 2016. doi:10.4230/LIPIcs.ECOOP.2016.13. Review of object inheritance for prototypes. Discusses multiple inheritance, but fails to cite KRL, Director, ThingLab, T, Slate, Sheeple. Only passingly discusses super linearization or mixin inheritance. Sad.
Kenneth Michael Kahn. An Actor-Based Computer Animation Language. In Proc. ACM/SIGGRAPH Workshop on User-Oriented Design of Interactive Graphics Systems, UODIGS ’76, pp. 37–43. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 1976. doi:10.1145/1024273.1024278. Kahn describes his yet unnamed language inspired by Hewitt’s actors (PLASMA) and Smalltalk-72, which would evolve into the language later called “Director”. In modern terms it is prototype-based, though Kahn himself uses class-and-instance terminology for what, in modern terms, is a prototype-based system: An object has a “parent” and possibly “children” (single inheritance is described; “inheritance of properties” is used); the word “class” at times seems to be used as synonym for “parent”. Kahn cites Kay, and Hewitt, but not Bobrow and Winograd (though he later does in his thesis).
Kenneth Michael Kahn. Creation of computer animation from story descriptions. PhD dissertation, MIT, 1979a. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/16012 This thesis is about the higher-level system Ani, which generates turtle graphics plans on top of the actor-based object system Director (see AIM-482b). Ani is a constraint solver based on a knowledge representation of the film being directed: a very crude 2D film with polygons as "performers" that move toward, away from, around or between one another, at various speeds appropriate to the action, as humans would on a stage. Kahn cites Bobrow & Winograd, as well as Kay, Hewitt, Lieberman, and many more (Licklider, Catmull!)
Kenneth Michael Kahn. Director Guide. MIT, AIM-482b, 1979b. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/6302 This paper, revised from a previous 1978 edition, presents Director, the earliest Lisp OO programming system as such, where inheritance exists in a programming context, not just in the knowledge representation context from which it evolved; see Kahn 1976. By then, Director had been factored out as the actor language underlying Kahn’s wider animation project Ani. Director implements single inheritance by passing unhandled messages to a parent actor, with the initial receiver’s identity as first argument. An actor knows its parent, offspring, descendants, siblings and childless-descendants as special variables (only the word “ancestor” does not appear). Director has an early form of call-next-method called continue-asking (p.40). The Actor team would later adapt Kahn’s inheritance mechanism under the name “delegation”; see Hewitt 1979. Kahn cites Smalltalk and Actors as influences for Director, but not KRL (Kahn does cite KRL in his thesis).
Samuel N. Kamin. Inheritance in Smalltalk-80: A Denotational Definition. In Proc. POPL, 1988. doi:10.1145/73560.73567. With Reddy 1988, one of the very first formal semantics for OO, with a simplified static model of Smalltalk-80 with single inheritance. Kamin uses syntactic rewrite rules, that he directly translated into a running ML program. This paper deserves much praise for being a first of its genre, translating a foreign paradigm in the vocabulary of FP, and being constructive with an actual running implementation based on U-encoding. In a way, the paper does too much by trying to have a realistic subset of Smalltalk, and too little by spending too little time explaining its dense model of inheritance, indeed as the fixpoint of the hierarchy of class definitions. But that’s OK, because Reddy 1988 is a very complementary paper that explains the concepts behind Kamin.
Samuel N. Kamin and Uday S. Reddy. Two Semantic Models of Object-Oriented Languages. In Theoretical Aspects of Object-Oriented Programming: Types, Semantics, and Language Design Chapter 13, Carl A. Gunter and John C. Mitchell (Ed.), Foundations of Computing, pp. 463–496. The MIT Press, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1994. https://openlibrary.org/books/OL1419064M/Theoretical_aspects_of_object-oriented_programming Kamin and Reddy join forces once again after their famous 1988 papers, and explicitly compare updated versions of their two semantic models of OO. The paper is heavy on formalism, which in the end drowns rather than highlights its beautiful conclusion: the equivalence between what they finally call the fixed-point model and the self-application model—what in this book I call Y-encoding and U-encoding.
I feel the paper is important enough that it deserves my nitpicking everything wrong about it—because, when stripped from those inessential mistakes, the paper really shines for its essential achievement.
As for the complexity of the paper: the authors independently implement classes in both models, rather than factoring out their common specification machinery, which requires two separate layers of scaffolding whose equivalence must then be proved. My presentation is much simpler for accepting specifications as more fundamental than classes; equivalence between the two encodings becomes trivial, and the scaffolding for classes on top of specifications can be built once and shared between encodings.
Also, Kamin and Reddy for most of the paper call the two models respectively “closure semantics” and “data structure semantics”, because the Y-encoding of Reddy 1988, like those of Cook 1987 and my chapter 5, involves representing records as functions (closures) so as to directly invoke a fixpoint operator, whereas the U-encoding from Kamin 1988, like most low-level implementations all the way back to Sutherland 1963, represents objects as records of instance variables plus a reference to the type descriptor containing the methods, where each method is explicitly passed the record as argument.
But this is a trivial accident of their models, independent of the essential distinction between Y-encoding and U-encoding. Steels 1983 shows you can do U-encoding with closures whereas my Rideau 2020 shows you can do Y-encoding with records. (And Abelson 1984 shows you can have records-as-closures without either Y- or U-encoding.) Note that Kiselyov 2005 and Simons 2015 also do kind of Y-encoding with records, but both use lazy languages, where recursively defined values of any type, including records, are considerably easier to construct, making that less remarkable than it sounds. In any case, they get the naming right in the end—but I want the reader to avoid being misled by this accident.
Finally, the authors claim that Y-encoding is more abstract than U-encoding. I admit I thought so too at first, but surprisingly they are wrong to generalize from the particular semantic domains of their separately constructed class models to the encodings themselves: purely local transformations can translate between the two encodings at the level of open object specifications, independently of any class scaffolding built on top of them. Thus, neither encoding is intrinsically more abstract than the other. Recovering these transformations is left as a fun exercise to the reader (solutions are available in pommette, the code accompanying this book).
Mark Kantrowitz. Portable Utilities for Common Lisp. School of Computer Science, Carnegie-Mellon University, CMU-CS-91-143, 1991. https://cl-pdx.com/static/CMU-CS-91-143.pdf A collection of portable free software utilities in Common Lisp, among which the first non-proprietary reimplementation of DEFSYSTEM (later known as MK-DEFSYSTEM to distinguish it from others), the only one until ASDF. Making the code portable across platforms that are not very well-defined with respect to files and processes, without a well-compartmentalized portability layer, makes for a lot of bad corner cases, and is difficult to refactor after the live knowledge of what exactly the code is supposed to mean is gone. So after Mark stopped maintaining, it was hard for maintainer to handle the bitrot, leading to a reimplementation from scratch, ASDF (for which I separated and documented a well-defined portability layer).
Alan Kay. The Early History of Smalltalk. In History of programming languages—II 28(3), pp. 511–598. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 1993. doi:10.1145/155360.155364. Great read about Smalltalk. Inheritance is discussed in section 11.5.1: Simula-style inheritance was deliberately left out of Kay’s work on FLEX and early Smalltalk. Kay credits Larry Tesler (slot inheritance), Henry Lieberman (delegation), and Bobrow and Winograd’s KRL (Frames), for the invention of Smalltalk inheritance.
Alan Kay. Clarification of “object-oriented” (email). 2003. https://www.purl.org/stefan_ram/pub/doc_kay_oop_en (accessed 2026-02-11). Alan Kay recollects the influences that led him to invent Object-Oriented Programming in an email to Stefan Ram.
Alan Kay. What thought process would lead one to invent Object-Oriented Programming? 2020. https://www.quora.com/What-thought-process-would-lead-one-to-invent-object-oriented-programming/answer/Alan-Kay-11 (accessed 2026-01-18). Kay answered lots of questions on Quora. This is one of his many answers. You can explore more. Very interesting from a historical point of view.
Sonya E. Keene. Object-Oriented programming in Common Lisp; A Programmer’s Guide to CLOS. New York : Addison-Wesley, 1989.
Andrew J. Kennedy and Benjamin C. Pierce. On Decidability of Nominal Subtyping with Variance. In Proc. International Workshop on Foundations and Developments of Object-Oriented Languages (FOOL/WOOD), 2007. https://www.cis.upenn.edu/~bcpierce/papers/variance.pdf Proves undecidability of nominal subtyping with variance in general, identifies three features whose combination is responsible, and characterizes decidable fragments covering .NET. Conjectures decidability for Java and Scala.
Gregor Kiczales, Jim Des Rivières, and Daniel G. Bobrow. The Art of the Meta-Object Protocol. MIT Press, 1991. https://direct.mit.edu/books/book/2607/The-Art-of-the-Metaobject-Protocol This classic book, often known as AMOP, describes how the implementation of an OO system can itself use OO, making it extensible using itself, which can be used both for richer semantics and higher performance. The feat requires a few manually tied loops to bootstrap the system. Beautiful. Many Common Lisp implementations have adopted some variant of this design, even though it was rejected from the Common Lisp standard itself.
Gregor Kiczales, Erik Hilsdale, Jim Hugunin, Mik Kersten, Jeffrey Palm, and William G. Griswold. An Overview of AspectJ. In Proc. ECOOP 2001 — Object-Oriented Programming, 15th European Conference, Budapest, Hungary, June 18-22, 2001, Proceedings, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, 2072, pp. 327–353. Springer, 2001. doi:10.1007/3-540-45337-7_18. The canonical reference for AspectJ, the most widely adopted AOP system/extension to Java. Shows AOP in practice when the 1997 paper remains on the theoretical side.
Gregor Kiczales, John Lamping, Anurag Mendhekar, Chris Maeda, Cristina Videira Lopes, Jean-Marc Loingtier, and John Irwin. Aspect-Oriented Programming. In Proc. ECOOP’97 — Object-Oriented Programming, 11th European Conference, Jyväskylä, Finland, June 9-13, 1997, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, 1241, pp. 220–242. Springer, 1997. doi:10.1007/BFb0053381. This is the original, defining paper for Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP). It introduced the key ideas of cross-cutting concerns, aspects, join points, advice, and aspect weaving. Cross-cutting aspects are exactly what create combinatorial pressure on single inheritance, and can be solved with multiple inheritance and method combinations.
Roger King. My Cat Is Object-Oriented. In Object-Oriented Concepts, Databases, and Applications Chapter 2, Won Kim and Frederick H. Lochovsky (Ed.), ACM Press Frontier Series, pp. 23–30. ACM Press and Addison-Wesley, New York, NY, USA, 1989. doi:10.1145/63320.66469. King mocks loose definitions of OO based on random desirable properties, using the deliberately absurd example of classifying his cat as object-oriented. While King mostly focuses on the difference between OO and semantic models for databases, his more general point is valid for OO in general: An early warning that memetic success had already turned “object-oriented” into a hodgepodge based on marketing hype, for lack of a precise objective definition.
Oleg Kiselyov. Many Faces of the Fixed-Point Combinator. 2024. https://okmij.org/ftp/Computation/fixed-point-combinators.html (accessed 2026-01-18). Oleg is a genius whose every writing deserves being read. This page has collection of interesting snippets about the Y combinator. Started in the early 2000s, last updated in 2024 (as of my reading the page).
Oleg Kiselyov and Ralf Lämmel. Haskell’s overlooked object system. 2005. https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0509027 The magical Oleg shows that, actually, there is enough structural subtyping hidden in the Haskell typesystem to do precisely the kind of things people usually do with OO, with lists of types at the type-level to handle extensible record types. Though Oleg does not bother to implement multiple inheritance, some have implemented Quicksort at the type-level in Haskell, so topological sort with C4 is probably just some more type astronautics away. As compared to most OO papers that discuss theory only, or push their own ad hoc system, Oleg discusses pragmatics, and reuses someone else’s language, without having to change it, all by programming at the type-level. On the other hand, Oleg is well versed in the theory precisely because he does his practical work decades after the theorists wrote their papers.
Shriram Krishnamurthi. Programming Languages: Application and Interpretation. 1st edition. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA, 2008. https://plai.org/ This is a great book about Programming Languages in general, and I love SK. SK introduces objects as closures, and even prototypes, in chapter 10. But one thing he just doesn’t get is multiple inheritance (10.3.3). In 10.3.5 he introduces mixins as a mechanism on top of first-class single-inheritance classes, which certainly works, but to me feels like putting the cart before the ox. Great stuff outside OO, and even the OO is decent, but in the end, like many academics, SK doesn’t grok OO. (The third edition has some improvements, but is still not there.)
Bent Bruun Kristensen, Ole Lehrmann Madsen, Birger Møller-Pedersen, and Kristen Nygaard. The BETA programming language. Department of Computer Science, Aarhus University, DAIMI PB-229, 1987. doi:10.7146/dpb.v16i229.7578. BETA is the successor of Simula. It claims to unify classes, procedures, functions and types as a single abstraction mechanism called “patterns”. Patterns are restricted prototypes that conflate first-class target records-or-procedures with second-class specifications of those targets that can be used with single inheritance (later work by Agesen et al. 1989 would make BETA specifications first class too, and the successor gBeta (Ernst 2000) would further expand the semantics of records into prototypes with dynamic (mutable) inheritance).
A “do” body is executed when an object of the pattern is invoked, with inputs bound to variables from an “enter” part (if any), and outputs are computed from expressions specified by an “exit” part (if any). Multiple invocations of a given object will overwrite the enter variables and execute the body anew, and so the expected way to use a pattern P as a function is to invoke a new object &P at each function call, making the analogy between object and call frame tangible.
Inheritance works by extending a pattern and, recursively, any virtual subpatterns further-bound along with it, at each level generalizing Simula’s concatenation semantics: in each “do” block, an “inner” keyword may specify where to execute a subpattern’s additional “do” code (if there is no “inner”, then any descendant-provided code will be ignored and never executed, which is unlike Simula, and an improvement in this context). In BETA, ancestors control the execution of descendants’ extensions, whereas in other languages, descendants’ extensions override and control the execution of ancestor-provided code. BETA patterns are open recursive, and this(P) denotes the current P object when used within P or code lexically nested inside P, while “inner P” can execute descendant-provided body extensions. Ugly: any communication of information between descendant and ancestor “do” blocks must happen through side effects to lexically shared variables.
Particularly remarkable is the treatment of how inheritance interacts with lexical nesting of patterns (which generalizes to prototypes and classes in other languages): “virtual patterns” partake of the specialization structure of their enclosing pattern (unlike “pattern variables” later introduced—an is-a vs has-a distinction). The semantic infrastructure to do it right already existed in earlier prototype languages such as KRL or Act-1; but their authors don’t seem to have specifically noticed and examined the semantics of nested prototypes. The BETA team did it first, and the author of the successor gBeta gave understandable explanations of the phenomenon as “family polymorphism” (Ernst 2001). Unhappily, this achievement is mired by the authors trying to bolt an incoherent type theory on top of it: inspired by the absurd premise that subclassing is subtyping (the NNOOTT), further binding specializes virtual patterns monotonically (correct) but BETA simultaneously treats specialization of the enclosing pattern as subtyping (incorrect); thus if a virtual pattern occurs in an input position, the result is required to be covariant parameter specialization, which is absurd. Meanwhile their typechecker unifies types it shouldn’t by failing to distinguish between the same pattern instantiated in different enclosing objects and hence distinct lexical environments (e.g. x.V vs y.V). Ernst addresses these typing issues in gBeta.
The report is hard to read: the authors are in their own world, with their own vocabulary, syntax and semantics, and fail to try to reduce their semantics to something simple in terms of logic, or anything understandable by others. Nygaard, Kristensen, Madsen and soon Møller-Pedersen started the BETA project in 1976, when others already had better OO (except, it bears repeating, with regard to nested patterns). By the time their design stabilized around 1980, they were far behind the OO state of the art, and they never caught up with progress that came up after 1977. Quite underwhelming. They never entered a mutually beneficial dialogue with the rest of the OO world, wherein they could exchange ideas in a common formalism, import good ideas from others, export good ideas from them. Very sad waste of great talent by self-imposed intellectual isolation.
Also published in Shriver & Wegner (eds.), Research Directions in Object-Oriented Programming, MIT Press, 1987, pp. 7–48.
Stein Krogdahl. Multiple Inheritance in Simula-like Languages. BIT Numerical Mathematics 25(2), pp. 318–326, 1985. doi:10.1007/BF01934377. Krogdahl extends Simula’s single-inheritance “prefix” mechanism to support multiple prefixes... but only for tree-shaped ancestries. Quite lame, especially since he cites both Borning and Cannon who did much better years earlier. He’s not even trying. But at least he doesn’t try to explode DAGs into trees like C++. This 1985 extension is obviously not part of Simula 67; it was not included in the 1986 Simula Standard, either, which retained single inheritance.
Butler W. Lampson. Hints for Computer System Design. In Proc. Proceedings of the 9th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, pp. 33–48. ACM, 1983. doi:10.1145/800217.806614. A collection of practical principles for designing computer systems, distilled from Lampson’s experience at Xerox PARC and elsewhere.
Julia L. Lawall and Daniel P. Friedman. Embedding the Self Language in Scheme. Computer Science Department, Indiana University, TR-276, 1989. https://scholarworks.iu.edu/dspace/items/73ab556f-b16e-42df-859d-da17f3ddcef6 This paper re-implements the prototype object system of Self in Scheme, thereby making its semantics more understandable. This notably includes mutable slots, cloning, mutable inheritance, method resolution depth-first without backtracking along the what Ungar calls the “sender path”. If the result doesn’t look quite so simple after all, it is because Self isn’t as simple conceptually as it aims to be; authors confuse length of low-level code for ease of reasoning at a high-level. A prototype object system in Scheme can be vastly simpler to implement as well as reason about (see T and YASOS, or the code in this book).
Primo Levi. Se questo è un uomo. De Silva, 1947. This book impressed me when I read it as a young man (in a French translation), and the words “Hier ist kein warum!” (Here there is no why!) still haunt me: the reply of a guard who snatched an icicle from the desperately thirsty Levi when he asked why. A 1959 translation to English by Stuart Woolf was published as “If this is a man”, or in US editions “Survival in Auschwitz”.
Henry Lieberman. Using Prototypical Objects to Implement Shared Behavior in Object-Oriented Systems. In Proc. Proceedings of the 1986 ACM Conference on Object-Oriented Programming Systems, Languages and Applications (OOPSLA ’86), pp. 214–223. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 1986. doi:10.1145/28697.28718. This is a rightly influential paper about Prototype OO, as compared to Class OO.
Lieberman starts with the philosophical underpinnings of these two complexes of ideas, which are quite interesting from a historical and psychological point of view, but have little relevance to a technical discussion decades later on the semantics of OO, its proper use or implementation. He then contrasts how the two OO paradigms are typically used to represent knowledge, how they compare in expressiveness, efficiency, concurrency issues and suitability for interactive use. He even explains (section 6) how to implement inheritance (i.e. Classes) in terms of delegation (i.e. Prototypes) and why a correspondence in the other direction is impossible (because inheritance depends only on the class, known before the instance is bound; the same argument as my “inheritance happens only at compile-time for 2nd-class classes, whereas prototypes need it at runtime”, but with a finer-grained staging of computation “times”).
Sadly, this great paper has been largely cited for the one bad take of its author: Lieberman unhelpfully identifies Prototype OO and Class OO with the respective underlying “delegation” and “inheritance” mechanisms, rather than distinguishing the nature of the targets of otherwise identical specification mechanisms.
Barbara Liskov. Data Abstraction and Hierarchy. In Proc. OOPSLA ’87, pp. 17–34. ACM, 1987. doi:10.1145/62138.62141. In her invited talk at OOPSLA, Liskov in section 3 promptly dismissed inheritance of implementation as “violating encapsulation”, a quick hack that doesn’t fit her semantic model focused on subtyping. She obviously does not understand the purpose and semantics on inheritance, falls deep into the NNOOTT, and with inheritance of implementation dismisses any actual OO. And yet, the same paper first introduces a variant of her now famous “Liskov substitution principle”. So, is it a bad paper? Was it wrong to invite her at OOPSLA? Not at all. She is a great influential researcher who deserved her Turing Award. But was her talk good about OO? Not at all either. It was a good talk at OOPSLA, just not one about OO.
Barbara Liskov. A History of CLU. In Jr. Thomas J. Bergin and Jr. Richard G. Gibson (Ed.), Proc. History of Programming Languages—II, pp. 471–510. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 1993. doi:10.1145/154766.155367. Liskov’s retrospective account of the development of data abstraction and CLU (previously MIT LCS-TR-561 report from 1992). It presents CLU as the first implemented language providing direct linguistic support for data abstraction and discusses its relationship to the distinct object-oriented tradition. Liskov is careful to distinguish her meaning for object-oriented (Wegner’s and my “object-based”) under which CLU is OO, from what she reckons is the more common meaning that includes inheritance.
William M. Lonergan and Paul A. King. Design of the B5000 System. Datamation 7(5), pp. 28–32, 1961. https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~kubitron/courses/cs252-S12/handouts/papers/b5000.pdf The paper presents the Burroughs B5000 computer architecture, one of the sources of inspiration cited by Alan Kay. It features a push-down stack (with “right-hand” Polish notation, prefiguring FORTH’s stack/RPN execution model); “independence of addressing” (memory position-independence for both code and data) through a “program reference table” (a relocatable table of values and descriptors for indirect access to data and program segments, prefiguring later linkage tables and, more distantly, some of the indirection mechanisms used for object dispatch, as well as execution environments and capability namespaces).
Augusta Ada Lovelace. Notes [on translation of Luigi Federico Menabrae’s paper on Babbage’s Analytical Engine]. In Richard Taylor’s Scientific Memoirs pp. 666–731. Richard and John E. Taylor, 1843. https://www.google.com/books/edition/Scientific_Memoirs_Selected_from_the_Tra/qsY-AAAAYAAJ?gbpv=1&pg=PA666 This paper is verily the foundation of all Computer Science, which should rightfully be called by the name Lovelace baptized it: “the science of operations”.
Ada Augusta King, Countess of Lovelace, translates to English an article (in French) about the Babbage Analytical Engine, by Luigi Menabrea, who would later become Prime Minister of newly unified Italy; and her translator’s notes are fantastic. Only her initials appear (A.A.L, at one point mistyped A.L.L.), because a woman, especially a noble one, shall not write, especially not on such lowly topics. But my! Her understanding of “operations”, the general notion of pure computation, is better than that of most computer scientists of today.
“First the symbols of operation are frequently also the symbols of the results of operations. We may say that symbols are apt to have both a retrospective and a prospective signification. […]” She groks both that there is a conflation of multiple meanings, and that it is good, yet can lead to confusion if not made explicit: past vs future, passive vs active, values vs continuations. She also anticipates symbolic computing: “symbolical” vs “numerical” “results” or “data” (outputs or inputs); and the dual use of symbols as code and data: “the symbols of numerical magnitude, are frequently also the symbols of operations”.
She understands that programmability (she lacks the word) makes the Analytical engine vastly superior to the fixed-purpose Difference Engine, indeed makes it “the executive right hand of abstract algebra”. She also confronts the problem that a variable may take multiple values during an execution, and proposes an elegant solution, using a superscript to the left of a variable to number each successive binding, turning them into actual mathematical variables again. Way more advanced than most computer scientists even today. Prescient.
Yuri I. Manin. Mathematics as Metaphor. American Mathematical Society, 2007. doi:10.1093/philmat/nkn013. This collection of writings about mathematics includes a nice Foreword by Freeman Dyson.
Scott Meyers. Effective C++: 50 Specific Ways to Improve Your Programs and Designs. Addison-Wesley Professional Computing Series. Addison-Wesley, Reading, MA, USA, 1992. An influential collection of design and programming guidelines for how to use C++. Solid practical advice, rooted in language knowledge and experience, at the right level of abstraction for users of the language. At times, theory could have helped simplify the discourse, but the book is consistent in its style and level of abstraction, which is overall more valuable. Its chapter on “Inheritance and Object-Oriented Design” is of a similar caliber: solid, practical, no-nonsense, based on solid understanding of the language, without taking sides on theoretical debates. It explicitly distinguishes public inheritance as modeling an “isa” relationship from “layering” (what others call aggregation or composition) as modeling either “has-a” or “is-implemented-in-terms-of”. The difference between the latter being that “has-a” cleanly exports the component and its interface as a member, whereas “is-implemented-in-terms-of” is about a hidden internal choice of representation that does not export its interface and could be replaced. Meyers explains that private inheritance in C++ is another way to model “is-implemented-in-terms-of”.
Matthew Might, Yannis Smaragdakis, and David Van Horn. Resolving and exploiting the k-CFA paradox: illuminating functional vs. object-oriented program analysis. In Proc. Proceedings of the 31st ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation, PLDI ’10, pp. 305–315. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 2010. doi:10.1145/1806596.1806631. The authors note how the complexity of k-CFA (Control Flow Analysis with context of depth k) was proven EXPTIME-complete for FP, yet polynomial for OOP; they then explain the difference as actually being about treatment of scopes, that are flattened by the requirement in typical OO languages that closures be created by explicitly creating objects with plenty of variables at once, when in FP (especially so with curried functions) you may get an exponential number of abstract nested closure values per number of variables. The flattened environment representation in OOP loses precision in exchange for a gain in execution speed. The same representation is possible in FP, using flattened environments rather than shared DAGs of scopes. From an abstract argument about complexity, the authors thus identify concrete improvements to algorithms for program representation and analysis. The correspondence between program analysis, abstract interpretation, and typesystems, may also suggest how this affects the complexity of types for OO in a closed program being optimized vs an open program being extended.
Marvin Minsky. A Framework for Representing Knowledge. MIT, AIM-306, 1974. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/6089 Minsky describes his ideas on how to represent knowledge in a computer as part of his project for Artificial Intelligence, in terms of structured “frames” representing stereotyped situations, linked into frame-systems and containing slots, defaults and procedural information. Minsky even uses the words “prototype” and “inherit”, but entirely incidentally, and NOT AT ALL to refer to the concepts at stake for OO.
John C. Mitchell and Gordon D. Plotkin. Abstract Types have Existential Type. In Proc. Proceedings of the 12th ACM Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL ’85), pp. 37–51, 1985. doi:10.1145/318593.318606. The title of this key paper captures the core contribution: implementations of abstract data types, consisting of a representation type and operations on it (i.e. modules), can hide their actual representation type you should think of abstract types for data and functions that operate on them (i.e. modules) as hiding the actual underlying type behind an existential quantifier. This enables reasoning about modules as first-class values in a second-order λ-calculus. An extended journal version was published in TOPLAS 10(3), 1988.
Torben Ægidius Mogensen. Self-Applicable Online Partial Evaluation of the Pure Lambda-Calculus. In Proc. 1995 ACM SIGPLAN Symposium on Partial Evaluation and Semantics-Based Program Manipulation, pp. 39–44, 1995. doi:10.1145/215465.215469. M encodes of the λ-calculus in itself using higher-order syntax, then has interpreters, reducers and partial evaluators for the encoding, and Futamura projections for those partial evaluators, and interactions with the Y combinator. Very cool stuff. Not directly related to OO, though. Also the representation choosen deliberately does not expose the sharing or non-sharing of nodes during graph reduction and evaluation; it is a “shallow” encoding in this way, which is actually great for many applications (where these details are a bore), and terrible for other applications (where these details are crucial).
Eugenio Moggi. Notions of computation and monads. Information and computation 93(1), pp. 55–92, 1991. doi:10.1016/0890-5401(91)90052-4. This seminal paper that explains how computations with all kinds of side effects can be expressed on top of the pure λ-calculus using monads. Though presented as an abstract tool for reasoning about the semantics of programming languages, the technique would quickly be adapted as the concrete basis for how Haskell exposes side effects indeed. Math heavy with category theory diagrams.
David A. Moon. Object-Oriented Programming with Flavors. SIGPLAN Not. 21(11), pp. 1–8, 1986. doi:10.1145/960112.28698. According to Gabriel 2012, this was “the first engineering publication about mixins” (in the Lisp sense, as introduced by Flavors), whereas Cannon’s 1979 report (this paper cites a 1982 copy) was privately circulated, mostly in Lisp circles at MIT and beyond (however, the Lisp Machine Manual from 1981 onward includes a chapter on Flavors).
This paper describes the New Flavors system from Symbolics, after it acquired the new “generic function” syntax, respect for local precedence order, and other niceties. Moon rightfully insists on the modularity advantage of Flavors (already mentioned by Cannon). This is a fantastic explanation of how to do multiple inheritance right, only way too short.
Oscar Nierstrasz. Ten Things I Hate About Object-Oriented Programming. Journal of Object Technology 9(5), pp. 5–16, 2010. doi:10.5381/jot.2010.9.5.e1. Nierstrasz is an OOP researcher in the Smalltalk tradition. In this provocative essay, he criticizes a few things about how OO is commonly practiced. The criticism is not always about OO itself, though sometimes it is; and whether it hits or misses, it certainly brings challenging thoughts and can inspire directions for future R&D.
Martin Odersky and Matthias Zenger. Scalable component abstractions. In Proc. 20th Annual ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Object-Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages, and Applications, OOPSLA ’05, 40(10), pp. 41–57. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 2005. doi:10.1145/1103845.1094815. This paper describes the OO and FP model of Scala 2 (then being developed), its flavorful multiple inheritance and its typesystem, with self-types and recursive type constraints. Imperfect as it may be (e.g. lack of C3, proper tail calls, and compromises to fit Java and the JVM), Scala has by far the best integration of OO, FP and types.
Chris Okasaki. Purely Functional Data Structures. PhD dissertation, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, 1996. https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~rwh/students/okasaki.pdf Okasaki’s PhD thesis, his original presentation of persistent purely functional data structures based on structural sharing and amortized analysis. It was later expanded into a great 1998 book with same title. A classic, greatly recommended.
Chris Okasaki and Andy Gill. Fast Mergeable Integer Maps. In Proc. Proceedings of the ACM SIGPLAN Workshop on ML, pp. 77–86, 1998. http://www.ittc.ku.edu/csdl/fpg/files/Okasaki-98-IntMap.pdf Original paper for a pure functional variant of big-endian Patricia tree (a.k.a. trie), an efficient and popular way to represent finite maps indexed by integers (that themselves could be the values of a hash function).
Bruno C. d. S. Oliveira. The Different Aspects of Monads and Mixins. Oxford University Computing Laboratory, 2009. https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/publications/publication2965-abstract.html Oliveira shows that there is enough subtyping in Haskell typeclasses for cool applications of Mixins, even without resorting to the type astronautics of Kiselyov 2005 or Gale 2015. A very nice paper on Mixins, though short of being capable of typing OO.
Harold Ossher and William Harrison. Combination of Inheritance Hierarchies. In Proc. Conference Proceedings on Object-Oriented Programming Systems, Languages, and Applications, OOPSLA ’92, pp. 25–40. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 1992. doi:10.1145/141936.141940. The authors present the point of view of OO as being used to extend not just individual classes, but class hierarchies. They call “extension-as-addition” what I call extensibility, or maybe modular extensibility (unclear which, but in the end what they extend are indeed modular entities, classes and class hierarchies). They discuss strategies to avoid “conflict” between independent extensions.
Russell O’Connor. Polymorphic Update with van Laarhoven Lenses. 2012. http://r6.ca/blog/20120623T104901Z.html (accessed 2025-12-01). Classic essay on functional lenses.
Bryan O’Sullivan, John Goerzen, and Donald Bruce Stewart. Real World Haskell. O’Reilly Media, 2008. doi:10.5555/1523280. This book demonstrates how Haskell by 2008 had grown into a practical language usable to write “Real World” applications.
D. L. Parnas. On the Criteria to Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules. Commun. ACM 15(12), pp. 1053–1058, 1972. doi:10.1145/361598.361623. A truly classic paper on modularity and the source of the information-hiding criterion: decompose a system around design decisions likely to change, hiding each such “secret” behind a stable interface. Using two competing decompositions of the same KWIC system, Parnas argues that modularization around the processing steps of a flowchart decomposition is inferior to modularization around hidden design decisions likely to change, because the latter permits modules to be understood and modified more independently.
John Peterson and Mark Jones. Implementing Type Classes. In Proc. ACM SIGPLAN Symposium on Programming Language Design and Implementation. Elsevier Science, 1993. http://web.cecs.pdx.edu/~mpj/pubs/pldi93.html A classic paper on how to implement typeclasses in Haskell, by desugaring them into extra dictionary arguments in a core calculus that does not have typeclasses.
Tomas Petricek. Miscomputation in software: Learning to live with errors. The Art, Science, and Engineering of Programming 1(2), 2017. doi:10.22152/programming-journal.org/2017/1/14. The author has a fascinating discussion on how programmers tend to each fall into one of a few very distinctive mindsets about programming, that lead to very different software development practices, and very different software artefacts, very different explanations about what software is, what it is for, and how to implement and use it.
Tomas Petricek. Cultures of Programming: The Development of Programming Concepts and Methodologies. Cambridge University Press, 2025. doi:10.1017/9781009492379. The author extends his earlier study (Petricek 2017) into a larger treatise on the distinct cultures that grew around opposite mindsets about programming.
Matthew Pickering, Jeremy Gibbons, and Nicolas Wu. Profunctor Optics: Modular Data Accessors. The Art, Science, and Engineering of Programming 1(2), 2017. doi:10.22152/programming-journal.org/2017/1/7. The paper generalizes lenses, prisms, traversals and other kinds of “functional optics” in terms of profunctors.
Benjamin C. Pierce. Bounded Quantification is Undecidable. In Proc. Proceedings of the 19th ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL). ACM, 1992. doi:10.1145/143165.143228. While it was known that you could type OO with a combination of subtyping and quantification over bounded types, Pierce importantly proves that this combination leads to type checking being undecidable. That means that in practice, more restrictive combinations are needed to usefully type objects. (See also 1994 journal version Information and Computation.)
Benjamin C. Pierce. Types and Programming Languages. 1st edition. MIT Press, 2002. https://www.cis.upenn.edu/~bcpierce/tapl/ TAPL treats objects in chapters 18, 19, 24, 32. 18 has a gradual approach to implementing not-quite-objects, and adding features until the reader has actually implemented objects. It’s clever, but a bit long-winded; also see my note on Pierce & Turner 1993 regarding letting the user provide a rep type. 32.10 Pierce does discuss the actual solution, recursive data types, but leaves it as an exercise after pointing to the bibliography. Pierce is technically masterful, but my impression is that he doesn’t understand the purpose of OO, because it is a foreign paradigm (see Gabriel 2012); and so not only he cannot drill into the essence of it, he spends more time on the non-essentials (imperative programming), and leaves the actually interesting essential (recursive types) out of his text, using a shortcut (his rep type) to survive without it.
Benjamin C. Pierce and David N. Turner. Simple Type-Theoretic Foundations for Object-Oriented Programming. 1993. https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-functional-programming/article/simple-typetheoretic-foundations-for-objectoriented-programming/5C18E2E055B028F7214FBB183701830E This is a solid paper worth reading, though I staunchly disagree with both the “Simple” and “Foundations” in the title. Pierce and Turner do not provide solid foundations that pin-point the essence of all OO, based on which to build any OO system. Instead, they show how you can side-step some of the really hard problems in OO (recursive types!), yet achieve most of the value in practice, using existential types for modularity: they push the problematic fixpoint into a corner, and ask the user to tie the knot manually in a case where it’s relatively easy for the user to do; then their system handles the rest and does the heavy lifting from there. Users can then achieve most of the benefits of OO despite the system being unable to tie the knot and solve the problem automatically. It is a “tell me what you need, I’ll show you how to do without!” kind of paper. And you shouldn’t take this description disparagingly: this is a great kind of paper, one that shows you how to do more with less. Brilliant and insightful. Yet, ultimately, an utter failure at the task its set upon itself, since it dodges rather than solves the problem announced in its title. Journal version in JFP(4)2, 1994.
Kent Pitman. Common Lisp HyperSpec. 1996. https://www.lispworks.com/documentation/HyperSpec/Front/index.htm (accessed 2026-01-06). The Common Lisp HyperSpec, or CLHS, is a carefully digitized version of the ANSI Common Lisp standard, the final draft of which was approved by X3J13 on December 8, 1994. It is fully clickable, includes the (non-binding, but enlightening) “issue writeups” that explain some of the design decisions, etc. Objects are described in chapter 7. Importantly, the document is meant as a reference, and not as a tutorial. You will have a hard time learning how to use Common Lisp in general or CLOS in particular by reading this document. But you can read tutorials, look at plenty of working examples in free software libraries, and then make sense of the finer details by reading the CLHS. Graham’s ANSI Common Lisp, Seibel’s Practical Common Lisp, the Common Lisp Cookbook, (or I’m told the OOP in CL by Keene) might be better to start learning; and CLtL2 or AMOP once you’re more advanced.
Sergiy Prykhodko, Natalia Prykhodko, and Smykodub Tatiana. A Statistical Evaluation of The Depth of Inheritance Tree Metric for Open-Source Applications Developed in Java. Foundations of Computing and Decision Sciences 46, pp. 159–172, 2021. doi:10.2478/fcds-2021-0011. A study that shows how shallow single inheritance hierarchies are in Java open source code. A good contrast with my own examination of the depth of class hierarchies in CLOS.
Christian Queinnec. Lisp in Small Pieces. Cambridge University Press, 1996. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139172974. This classic book will demystify the implementation of languages in the Lisp or Scheme family. Great for theory and practice alike.
R7RS Working Group. Revised⁷ Report on the Algorithmic Language Scheme. Scheme Language Steering Committee, 2013. https://standards.scheme.org/official/r7rs.pdf Final R7RS-small report, announced at Scheme 2013 on July 6, 2013; archival ACM publication appeared in 2016. Latest version of the standard for the Scheme language.
Eric S. Raymond and others. The New Hacker’s Dictionary. 3rd edition. MIT Press, Cambridge, MA, 1996. http://www.catb.org/jargon/ Also known online as The Jargon File, a classic for all programmers. Foreword and cartoons by Guy L. Steele Jr. The website has various updates compared to the book, and is stable since 2003.
Uday Reddy. Objects as Closures - Abstract Semantics of Object Oriented Languages. In Proc. ACM Symposium on LISP and Functional Programming, pp. 289–297, 1988. doi:10.1145/62678.62721. This paper is a great sequel and complement to Kamin 1988. Where Kamin implemented a complete workable subset of Smalltalk-80, Reddy instead decomposes the concepts of OO into simpler concepts that he gradually extends. Reddy explains how to achieve OO with Y-encoding. Reddy doesn’t provide complete running code but notes that Kamin implemented Reddy’s variant as well as Kamin’s own. Together a great pair of paper.
Jonathan Rees. On Object-Oriented Programming. 2003. https://www.paulgraham.com/reesoo.html A response to Paul Graham about Object-Oriented Programming, critical of what the concept had come to mean and how it was abused in the industry at the time.
Jonathan A. Rees. A Security Kernel Based on the Lambda Calculus. PhD dissertation, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA, 1995. doi:10.5555/921818. Fantastic classic paper, Rees’s thesis introduces his “W7” security kernel, leveraging scoping as a natural mechanism for object capabilities based security.
Jonathan A. Rees and Norman I. Adams. T: a dialect of LISP or, Lambda: the ultimate software tool. In Proc. Symposium on Lisp and Functional Programming, ACM, pp. 114–122, 1982. doi:10.1145/800068.802142. A short overview of the Yale T Scheme system, a dialect of Lisp that is lexically scoped (which was not yet the norm at the time), and that among other things supports Prototype OO based on such lexically scoped closures. An object is essentially a record of methods that are invoked by passing them the object as first argument. A “generic operation protocol” offers a functional syntax for object method invocation, which anticipates generic functions in New Flavors, CommonLoops and CLOS. See Adams 1988 for details.
John C. Reynolds. Towards a Theory of Type Structure. In Proc. Colloque sur la Programmation, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, 19, pp. 408–425. Springer, 1974. doi:10.1007/3-540-06859-7_148. Reynolds’s famous paper independently introducing essentially the same polymorphic typed λ-calculus as Girard 1972’s System F.
John C. Reynolds. Three Approaches to Type Structure. In Proc. Mathematical Foundations of Software Development (TAPSOFT/CAAP), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, 185, pp. 97–138. Springer, 1985. doi:10.1007/3-540-15198-2_7. Reynolds notes the equivalence between three approaches to types in programming languages: Milner’s type deduction/inference system (Hindley-Milner with the polymorphic let); the theory of subtypes and generic operators (Reynolds’s own earlier work on implicit conversions via category theory); and the polymorphic/second-order typed λ-calculus (Girard’s logical System F). He illustrates all three in a common functional language with products, sums, and lists, comparing their expressiveness and trade-offs.
François-René Rideau. LIL: CLOS Reaches Higher-Order, Sheds Identity and has a Transformative Experience. In Proc. International Lisp Conference, 2012. http://github.com/fare/lil-ilc2012/ I show how to achieve parametric polymorphism in Common Lisp, by passing around “interfaces”, objects that describe some API. Interfaces are analogous to the “dictionaries” with which typeclasses are implemented in Haskell, or to first-class ML modules, except they integrate very well with the OO capabilities of CLOS. I then show not only how to write either “pure” or “stateful” variants of such interfaces, but how the two are equivalent, and can be automatically transformed into one another with macros. Similarly, macros can automatically transform between these “pure” or “stateful” interface in typeclass styles and respective “posh” or “classy” classes in traditional OO style. Typeclass vs class, pure vs stateful are then just a matter of expression style rather than of fundamentally different computing paradigms.
François-René Rideau. ASDF 3, or Why Lisp is Now an Acceptable Scripting Language. In Proc. European Lisp Symposium, 2014. https://github.com/fare/asdf3-2013 In this paper, I describe the build system ASDF, and its design, its evolution from ASDF 1 (and its predecessors) to ASDF 3, with surprising challenges from portability to extension of project scope, to a bug that was half-fixed in one line of code but required a complete rewrite for a real fix. The heart of ASDF is a protocol using plenty of multi-methods specialized on an operation and a component. The combination of flavorful multiple inheritance and multiple dispatch makes for an extremely modular and extensible design, that accomplishes in a few thousands of lines what other build systems do in tens or hundreds of thousands of lines of code.
François-René Rideau. Build Systems and Modularity. 2016. https://ngnghm.github.io/blog/2016/04/26/chapter-9-build-systems-and-modularity/ (accessed 2023-11-29). I once wrote a blog “Houyhnhnm Computing” (pronounced “Hunam”), wherein a Houyhnhnm (sentient equine creature such as the ones once visited by Gulliver in his travels) challenges mainstream human views on “Computer Science” from his alien point of view. That chapter was focused on build systems, and software support for modularity in general.
François-René Rideau. Climbing Up the Semantic Tower — at Runtime. In Proc. Off the Beaten Track Workshop at POPL, 2018a. https://github.com/fare/climbing A very short presentation of the concepts in the first part of my thesis: how to formalize the notion of implementation, what good properties to achieve, with a note on how this could lead to a runtime reflection protocol.
François-René Rideau. Reconciling Semantics and Reflection. 2018b. https://bit.ly/FarePhD Unpublished because undefended. First draft completed in 2018, yet still not in a publishable state as of 2026. In my thesis, I reconcile Semantics (knowing as much as possible about the meaning of a program before you even run it, which might not terminate) and Reflection (being able to modify a program and its meaning while it’s running), two seemingly antinomic concepts—by developing a protocol to negotiate what can be changed and what must be preserved about a given program. Thus, users can trust the integrity of the software they use, developers can debug the most difficult situations and update the software as needed, and administrators can ensure the software runs on affordable and reliable hardware, even as requirements evolve, computers age and economic conditions change. The thesis distinguishes three orthogonal axes of “reflection” that people commonly conflate or confuse: pre/post (code generation), hypo/hyper (semantic implementation), back/fore (runtime control). The thesis has four parts: The first part focuses on the notion of implementation, and the good properties one might expect from an implementation; one property is particularly important that everyone else neglects: observability. The second part shows how the same properties, well formalized, become a protocol for runtime reflection, wherein observability does the heavy lifting of synchronizing the system in a quiescent state that makes transformations possible. The third part explores what kind of existing practices can be simplified when explained in terms of such reflection protocol. The fourth part proposes a software architecture for reflective runtime control of software, based on the previous. The first two sound boring or trivial without the last two; the last two sound fantastic or impossible without the first two. And yet, the end result sounds simple and necessary once you have shifted your point of view from the common wisdom (or lack thereof) that most people induce from standard practice.
François-René Rideau. Gerbil-POO. 2020. https://github.com/fare/gerbil-poo (accessed 2021-04-06). A simple Prototype Object System on top of Gerbil Scheme, with flavorful multiple inheritance, in a mostly pure functional lazy style, yet also allowing for mutable state (though without support for dynamic changes in inheritance hierarchy). I implemented it initially as an exercise after discovering the Nix extension system, as a demonstration of how an object system could at the same time be radically simple and radically more expressive than all the others that had ever been written (thanks to both being first-class and having flavorful multiple inheritance). I liked the result so much that I used it in many software packages I wrote, achieving a level of simplicity and generality that was not available to me in Common Lisp, OCaml or Haskell (see for instance the trie implementation, and its merkleized extension in gerbil-persist).
François-René Rideau. Pure Object Prototypes. 2021. https://github.com/divnix/POP My implementation in Nix of a prototype object system with multiple inheritance.
François-René Rideau. c4-mixins. 2026. https://github.com/fare/c4-mixins My C++ implementation of optimal inheritance: header-only C++20 mixins with a c4-linearized “super” chain. Inspired by Smaragdakis 2000, with help from Claude to translate the C4 algorithm from Gerbil Scheme to about 1 kloc of C++ templates.
François-René Rideau and Robert Goldman. Evolving ASDF: More Cooperation, Less Coordination. In Proc. International Lisp Conference, 2010. doi:10.1145/1869643.1869648. In this report, I (then maintainer) and Robert (now maintainer) explain how we took over ASDF, the de facto standard build system for Common Lisp (successor to DEFSYSTEM, vaguely analogous to Make in C), and turned it into ASDF 2, making it vastly more usable: robust, portable (especially wrt pathnames), easy to configure, with support for caching fasls (output files) separately per implementation. A crucial technique that unlocked the social acceptability of new features was the ability to upgrade ASDF after installation: before that, users were locked with the vendor-provided version so had incentive to always support the worst version of ASDF, which means vendors had no incentive to upgrade. Dynamic upgradability reversed the incentives, illustrating the feedback between technology and social dynamics. In general, ASDF was made to better fulfill its role of supporting modularity, as characterized by the subtitle: more cooperation, less coordination.
François-René Rideau, Alex Knauth, and Nada Amin. Prototypes: Object-Orientation, Functionally. In Proc. Scheme and Functional Programming Workshop, 2021. https://github.com/metareflection/poof The original paper in which I describe my reconstruction of a minimal model of Prototype OO with mixin inheritance in the style of Jsonnet and Nix, and in which appears the very first full-throated conceptualization of conflation in OO.
Y.-J. Ringard. Mustard Watches: An Integrated Approach to Time and Food. Unpublished satirical manuscript, 1990. https://girard.perso.math.cnrs.fr/mustard/article.html Satirical parody of the proliferation of meaningless mathematical generalizations. Written by Jean-Yves Girard under the pseudonym “Y.-J. Ringard” and widely circulated informally.
Douglas T. Ross. A Generalized Technique for Symbol Manipulation and Numerical Calculation. Communications of the ACM 4(3), pp. 147–150, 1961. doi:10.1145/366199.366256. Introduces Ross’s plex representation—built from what we would today call records, or structs—a generalized structure in memory whose components may contain data, links (pointers to more data), or even code to jump to (not just a pointer to the address to jump to, but the actual transfer instruction, which can itself be jumped to and will then typically transfer control to the correct fixed-address subroutine). One of the tricks Ross proposes and names “reversed use of index register” consists in having a fixed offset from an object at a variable address in the register, whereas the normal usage expected by everyone else was a variable offset in the register to an object at a fixed address. Very clever and low-level—the paper also illustrates the level of abstraction at which most programmers were thinking at the time, for the paper to even be published.
Ross doesn’t say whether the index register is to be used as an argument by the code being jumped to—which would be an early example of what I’d call U-encoding. The indexed transfer certainly preserves the index register, and for the routine being called to reuse the value in that register rather than clobber it is the most natural extension of the idea, without even having to conceptualize it as an argument being passed. Who today can guess what was obvious or needed to be explicitly conceptualized at a time when Ross’s paper was worth publishing? At least Sutherland 1963 will make that notion explicit. Presented earlier at the ACM Conference on Symbolic Manipulation, May 20–21, 1960.
Douglas T. Ross. Toward foundations for the understanding of type. In Proc. Proceedings of the 1976 Conference on Data: Abstraction, Definition and Structure, pp. 63–65. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 1976. doi:10.1145/800237.807120. In an unreadable manic publication that is more “philosophy” than science, Ross gives one of the earliest uses in print (March 1976) of the word “object-oriented” in a way that vaguely refers to organizing language semantics around objects and types. But since it’s all poetic handwaving (despite the invocation of mathematical symbols), this publication can be dismissed as useless as a candidate for the first definition of OO.
Claudio V. Russo. Types for Modules. PhD dissertation, University of Edinburgh, 1998. https://era.ed.ac.uk/handle/1842/385 Russo adds first-class modules to ML, that only had second-class modules up until then. Includes a lot of work on the type system, admittedly more than I can follow.
Didier Rémy. Programming objects with ML-ART an extension to ML with abstract and record types. In Proc. International Symposium on Theoretical Aspects of Computer Software, pp. 321–346. Springer, 1994. doi:10.1145/263699.263707. Rémy uses extensible records and a form of existential types, plus “projective types” (to palliate lack for higher order kind *→*), to emulate what Pierce and Turner do with Fω≤. He implements flavorless multiple inheritance, with or without mutation. This is solid work as a typesystem, but not very usable as an object system, and the limited support for subtyping doesn’t help. Indeed, Rémy admits in a personal conversation (2026) that he was only interested in typesystems, not object systems. Yet, this work is the basis for what will be the O in OCaml. As I often jest, the O in OCaml actually stands for how much the authors of OCaml actually care about Objects.
Jerome H. Saltzer. The “Principle of Least Privilege” and Multics. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Project MAC, CSR-RFC 35, 1973. https://web.mit.edu/Saltzer/www/publications/rfc/csr-rfc-035.pdf An early explicit statement of the principle of least privilege, in the context of the Multics protection system, which Saltzer credits to David J. Edwards. It predates Saltzer and Schroeder’s influential 1975 presentation of least privilege as one of the fundamental design principles for protection systems. The principle was later generalized as the Principle of Least Authority (POLA) in capability-security literature.
Lee Salzman and Jonathan Aldrich. Prototypes with Multiple Dispatch: An Expressive and Dynamic Object Model. In Proc. ECOOP, 2005. doi:10.1007/11531142_14. For the Slate language, Lee implemented Prototypes with Multiple Dispatch (PMD), combining Prototype OO, multiple dispatch, and “dynamic inheritance” (mutable ancestry). Multi-methods are internalized as objects (as in the CLOS MOP), allowing more flexibility than an second-class dispatch mechanism across a static ancestry. In an invocation, each argument, an object, plays a role, that correspond to its argument position. Applicable methods are sorted in the total order of a depth-first traversal (with visited-set maintenance to avoid exponential duplicates) by argument position, time of method creation (for overrides), and method specificity; the ordering is a bit like linearization in CLOS, adapted to support dynamic inheritance. Some optimizations on traversing the applicable methods ensure that the usual case of single-dispatch is efficiently implemented as part of the regular multiple dispatch algorithm.e There is even support for subjective dispatch, with a global implicit additional argument on which to dispatch in zeroth position. All in all quite an interesting innovative design for method dispatch, maybe the most advanced and dynamic ever.
Andrew Shalit, David A. Moon, and Orca Starbuck. The Dylan Reference Manual: The Definitive Guide to the New Object-Oriented Dynamic Language. Addison-Wesley, 1996. doi:10.5555/236379. Dylan was an OO dynamic language developed at Apple for the Newton. But it wasn’t completed on time to write the Newton OS on, and Dylan was eventually cancelled. Dylan was built by Lisp hackers from MIT and Symbolics, and you can feel the influence of Common Lisp and Lisp Machine Lisp, but with a more familiar infix syntax, semantics that were streamlined and simplified, and a view on allowing delivery of compact, efficient executables. It had flavorful multiple inheritance with class linearization, but reintroduced conflict for multiple dispatch. It also introduced sealing, as a technique whereby users can specify that a set of classes could not be extended beyond the current file (more general and flexible than the final annotation of many OO languages). enabling various optimizations.
Michele Simionato. The Python 2.3 method resolution order. 2003. https://www.python.org/download/releases/2.3/mro/ (accessed 2026-02-26). This part of the Python documentations has plenty of examples for how the precedence list (that they call Method Resolution Order (MRO)) is computed using C3, though there are not that many explanations.
Anthony James Howard Simons. A Language with Class: The Theory of Classification Exemplified in an Object-Oriented Programming Language. PhD dissertation, University of Sheffield, Sheffield, UK, 1995. https://staffwww.dcs.shef.ac.uk/people/A.Simons/research/thesis/ Simons develops a “Theory of Classification” and exemplifies it in his Brunel 2.0 programming language. He notably models classes as open, higher-order F-bounded constructs in the λ-calculus, and distinguishes them from the types obtained as their least fixed points. His entire writing is very accessible, and his presentation of types is refreshingly clear and understandable compared to contemporary sources. He then studies inheritance, genericity, mixins, and multiple inheritance all in one framework, before he introduces the language that embodies his theory.
Simons is uniquely explicit in clearly distinguishing class and type, and in deploring their conflation in extent literature. (He also calls “naïve” the model of inheritance confusing it with subtyping.) He deserves big credits for his clairvoyance in this regard. Simons is also astute in noting that the “self” argument (a regular variable!) is an “alias” (reference) to an object of the desired type rather than directly such an object, which actually matters a lot in a typed applicative language; he fails to make the matter explicit, though, or to relate it to the situation of “this C” in Simula or “this” in C++.
On the other hand, Simons’ main weakness is that his type-first approach makes him completely miss on Prototype OO. He also gives too much of a role to type generators as opposed to mixins: mixins appear, briefly, but are never taken seriously as a central focus. Simons’ discussion of multiple inheritance is also lacking, and his mention of linearization is cursory.
Anthony James Howard Simons. The Theory of Classification. Journal of Object Technology, 20-part monograph series, vols. 1–4, 2002–2005, 2005. https://staffwww.dcs.shef.ac.uk/people/A.Simons/research/journal.html A twenty-part monograph on object-oriented type theory, published serially in the Journal of Object Technology from 2002 to 2005, expanding on Simons’s 1995 thesis. Simons goes through a lot of basics, addressing OO programmers who may not be all too familiar with the many formalisms he uses, making the text quite verbose as a whole. A good overview of a vast topic: types vs classes, subtyping vs subclassing, object encodings, recursive types, subtyping, inheritance, self-reference, super-reference, genericity, mixins and multiple inheritance.
Simons crucially understands the problem most programmers have with conflating types and classes, and the confusion that ensues; but he does not understand the modularity advantage of conflation when used without confusion—probably because his theory only covers classes and not prototypes, which is a shame. His treatment of mixins and multiple inheritance is also weak, as Simons clings to modular definitions (that he calls “type generators”) as the central entity of this theory, and only reluctantly uses modular extensions (“mixins”) when forced, without making them a subject of study as such, indeed spending a lot of energy making super a pseudo-variable rather than simply an actual variable.
Peter Simons. Nixpkgs fixed-points library. 2015. https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/master/lib/fixed-points.nix (accessed 2023-11-29). Nix implements prototype OO in two functions. Impressive. Seeing this system after having used Jsonnet (that implements an equivalent object system the hard way in C++, documented in two pages of semantic rules) is what made OO click for me. Peter doesn’t call his extension system “OO” and didn’t know about Prototype OO when he wrote that—but had been influenced by others who did. Nevertheless, his extensions are used exactly like objects are in Jsonnet, for sensibly the same purposes—configuring complex systems in a modular extensible way.
Yannis Smaragdakis and Don Batory. Mixin-based programming in C++. In Greg Butler and Stan Jarzabek (Ed.), Proc. International Symposium on Generative and Component-Based Software Engineering, pp. 164–178. Springer. Berlin, Heidelberg, 2000. doi:10.1007/3-540-44815-2_12. This paper very nice paper implements proper mixin inheritance on top of C++ using templates. Note that it does not try to implement ancestry linearization, and therefore does not implement flavorful multiple inheritance; though such linearization could probably be done on top of their mixin inheritance.
John Miles Smith and Diane C. P. Smith. Database Abstractions: Aggregation and Generalization. ACM Transactions on Database Systems 2(2), pp. 105–133, 1977. doi:10.1145/320544.320546. Identifies aggregation and generalization as two fundamental and independent abstractions for conceptual data modeling in the context of databases. Generalization organizes objects into hierarchies of generic objects, while aggregation constructs composite objects from relationships among objects. These anticipate the conceptual distinction later expressed in object-oriented terminology as “is-a” versus “has-a” or “part-of”, although Smith and Smith do not use those slogans. However, the lack of support for late-bound self-variables in types means this “generalization” only matches inheritance in the trivial case where the inherited structure does not recursively refer to its own type. See section 3.1.7.
Raymond Smullyan. To Mock a Mockingbird and Other Logic Puzzles: Including an Amazing Adventure in Combinatory Logic. Knopf, 1985. One of Smullyan’s many delightful narrated puzzle books that prove deeper than they look: “To Mock a Mockingbird” takes the reader through the essentials of combinatory logic. Each chapter introduces more elaborate logical ideas, until, starting with chapter 9, the book follows Inspector Craig as he explores the “birds” of various “forests”, the birds being combinators and the forests being sets of terms closed by application.
The self-application combinator, which I call U in this book, is called M (Mockingbird) in Smullyan’s. The fixpoint combinator (which I call Y) appears in chapter 10 as a Sage bird Θ, the same symbol Turing first used to denote such a combinator; though in chapter 13, Smullyan calls U the critical part of the Sage bird from Turing’s original paper (which is different from my U, Smullyan’s M).
Smullyan then shows how to express logic and arithmetic with combinators, and the book culminates in the final chapter, 25, with Gödel’s incompleteness theorem. The epilogue pleasantly notes that Moses Schönfinkel, whose work initiated what later became combinatory logic and the λ-calculus, bore a surname that in German literally means “beautiful bird”.
Alan Snyder. Encapsulation and Inheritance in Object-Oriented Programming Languages. In Proc. Conference Proceedings on Object-Oriented Programming Systems, Languages and Applications, OOPSLA ’86, pp. 38–45. Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 1986. doi:10.1145/28697.28702. This very well-informed, very interesting paper, and its extended version “Inheritance and the Development of Encapsulated Software Systems” in Research Directions in Object-Oriented Programming (1987), get a whole lot right about inheritance, yet get enough crucially wrong. Sadly, they are often cited for the wrong parts rather than the right parts.
Snyder systematically introduces parent, ancestor, child, descendant, as unambiguous names substituting for the awkward direct-superclass, superclass, direct-subclass, subclass. He identifies the importance of modularity, but fails to use that word, and instead somehow divides the concept into two separate properties “encapsulation” and “data abstraction”. He notes the need for reflection to defeat this encapsulation for debugging purposes.
Snyder has good discussions of inheritance, visibility, subtyping, etc. But multiple inheritance is a topic where Snyder majorly fails, despite his erudition. He calls “graph oriented solutions” the conflict view of multiple inheritance, and identifies many problems with it. He calls “linear solutions” the Flavors and CommonLoops view, and regrets the lack of conflict where he expects one, then regrets the lack of communication with “real” parents (but… that’s what defining more methods is for), so he wishes for the ability of “graph oriented solutions” to directly call another specific method (which is a terrible idea and, as he saw, didn’t work), and finally worries about name clashes (yes, but that’s not specific to “linear solutions”).
Dissatisfied for wrong reasons, and not having any theory of what OO should do and why, Snyder invents his own “tree solutions” for his system CommonObjects, trying to wish his simple tree to solve a problem that obviously requires a DAG, admitting his solution “radically changes the semantics of inheritance” and that “[f]urther experimentation is needed to determine the practicality of this alternative programming style”. In other words, he has no clue what he’s doing, tries something random because it is simple and convenient for him, and hopes his “solution” will stick. But for his “solution” to stick, his predecessors would have to have completely misidentified the problem, for reasons he cannot explain, since he is lacking a theory. That’s, well, not respectful of them or himself. Next time, don’t kick down Chesterton’s fence.
Now, what does it tell us that Stroustrup 1989 came up with essentially the same solution for C++, just with less research behind it? (At least Stroustrup also allowed virtual classes in addition to non-virtual one). Meanwhile, CommonObjects, the system Snyder is discussing, was written in Common Lisp, and COOL, its reimplementation on top of PCL (the first implementation of CLOS), can still be found.
Special Issue on Smalltalk. BYTE 6 (8), 1981. https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-Byte/80s/Byte-1981-08.pdf Special issue of BYTE devoted to Smalltalk-80, edited by Christopher P. Morgan, containing articles by Adele Goldberg, Dan Ingalls, Larry Tesler and other members of the Xerox Learning Research Group. Conspicuously absent from the list of authors is Alan Kay, who had left Xerox. The issue brought Smalltalk and object-oriented programming to a broad audience of microcomputer enthusiasts, and was an important milestone in popularizing the object-oriented paradigm.
James L Stansfield. COMEX: A Support System for a Commodities Expert. MIT, AIM-423, 1977. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/6281 An early expert system for trading commodities, written in FRL, a frame-based Lisp system, and organizing data in a knowledge base of frames. The paper is the earliest one to mention “single inheritance” and “multiple inheritance”, p.12 and p.13, about the frame representation of the COMEX data.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. LAMBDA: The Ultimate Declarative. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, AIM-379, 1976. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/6091 The second “Lambda the Ultimate” paper. It develops an efficient implementation model for λ-expressions and closures: LAMBDA is treated as an operator for GOTO combined with environment renaming. The paper shows how conventional control and environment constructs can be expressed in terms of λ-expressions and function invocation while preserving efficient execution, establishing the λ-calculus as a practical implementation substrate for high-level languages, not merely a theoretical formalism for their semantics. The paper also contains the striking section “Actors ≡ Closures (mod Syntax)”, explicitly identifying actors and closures at the implementation level.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. Debunking the “Expensive Procedure Call” Myth or, Procedure Call Implementations Considered Harmful or, LAMBDA: The Ultimate GOTO. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, AIM-443, 1977. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/5753 The third “Lambda the Ultimate” paper. It demolishes the folklore that procedure calls are inherently expensive, showing that tail calls can be compiled directly as GOTOs, and more generally that procedure calls can uniformly be regarded as GOTOs that pass parameters. It argues that cheap procedure calls can serve as a general control mechanism, capable even of expressing arbitrary flowcharts without explicit GOTOs, while separating abstract control concepts from the particular language constructs used to express them. A version was published in the Proceedings of the 1977 ACM Annual Conference, pp. 153–162.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. RABBIT: A Compiler for SCHEME (A Dialect of LISP). Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Technical Report, AI-TR-474, Cambridge, MA, 1978. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/6913 Steele presents his optimizing compiler for Scheme, a Lisp dialect with lexical scoping. After macro expansion and source-to-source transformations, source code is reduced to a small λ-calculus-based core that is compiled with procedure integration and tail-recursion optimization. Revised version of a Master’s dissertation submitted to the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. Common Lisp: The Language, 2nd edition. Digital Press, USA, 1990. doi:10.5555/1098646. This book, known as CLtL2, presents a snapshot of the work of X3J13, the committee that was standardizing ANSI Common Lisp.
While there are discrepancies between the contents of this book and the actual standard, a lot of the material is already there in essentially its final form. CLtL2 contains many features that were not included in the standard due to lack of consensus; nevertheless, many implementations also adopted these features in some form. Still, the standard is the actual reference document. On the other hand, the standard is dry, whereas CLtL2 is much more didactic. CLtL2 is thus a better introduction to the concepts, though it is not authoritative.
There was also a first edition of CLtL, back in 1984, but the language evolved a lot between the two editions, and the first edition came years before the Object System was designed. Objects are described in chapter 28 of CLtL2.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. It’s Time for a New Old Language. In Proc. Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGPLAN Symposium on Principles and Practice of Parallel Programming, pp. 1–1. ACM, Austin, Texas, USA, 2017. doi:10.1145/3018743.3018773. Steele identifies and analyzes “Computer Science Metanotation” (CSM), the informal symbolic language widely used in computer-science publications to define syntax, judgments, inference rules, substitution, repetition, etc. Steele shows how this ubiquitous yet previously unnamed language has evolved its own syntax, semantics and idioms, with ambiguities and inconsistencies. He offers an initial attempt to formalize the ill-defined language, and calls for interpreters, compilers, IDEs and proof checkers to support it. A more detailed treatment appears in his 2016 manuscript “Toward a More Carefully Specified Metanotation,” prepared for POPL 2017.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. and Richard P. Gabriel. The Evolution of Lisp. In Proc. Proceedings of the Second ACM SIGPLAN Conference on History of Programming Languages (HOPL-II), pp. 231–270, 1993. doi:10.1145/155360.155373. Gabriel and Steele discuss the evolution of Lisp and the essential concepts in it.
Guy Lewis Steele Jr. and Gerald Jay Sussman. LAMBDA: The Ultimate Imperative. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, AIM-353, 1976. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/5790 The first “Lambda the Ultimate” paper. It systematically shows how imperative control constructs can be expressed using λ-expressions, tail calls and continuations. The authors famously were trying to make sense of message dispatch in Hewitt’s Actors in terms of continuations; while building an experimental interpreter that intermixed actors and Lisp λ-expressions, they realized that the two were identical in implementation, and this realization had led to the design of Scheme.
Luc Steels. ORBIT: An Applicative View of Object-Oriented Programming. In Pierpaolo Degano and Erik Sandewall (Ed.), Proc.
